method: Research for this build was conducted with WebSearch. Direct WebFetch of primary docs (kafka.apache.org, avro.apache.org, docs.confluent.io, developer.confluent.io) was blocked by this environment's network egress policy, so the sources below were consulted through search-result extracts rather than fetched page text. Claims are therefore recorded at the level the extracts supported, and every version-specific number is listed under volatile[] for a later verify pass against the primary source.

structure.rationale: The requester's outline is deliberately contract-first: it teaches event contracts before mechanics, then uses mechanics to justify contract decisions. We keep all 25 chapters in the author's order and in six parts, because the arc is the pedagogy — internals (Part II) exist to make Part III's evolution rules feel inevitable rather than arbitrary, and the case studies (Part VI) are where the two halves finally meet. Installation and version history are excluded by explicit request. Every chapter ends by connecting a mechanism to a design decision, which is the book's stated differentiator.
structure.audience: Working engineers and architects building or operating event-driven systems on Kafka in an enterprise, who know how to produce and consume and now need to design contracts that survive years of independent deployment.

claims.text: A Kafka topic is a long-lived integration interface: retained records can be read by consumers written long after the producer, so an event's shape is a published API rather than an implementation detail.
Schema Registry governance is API governance, not merely tooling — compatibility policy decides who may break whom.
The default BACKWARD compatibility exists specifically so consumers can be rewound to the beginning of a topic and still read old data with a new schema.

pitfalls: Treating a topic as an internal queue between two services you own, then discovering a third team built on it.
Modeling events after database tables, which couples the contract to a schema you intended to refactor.
Conflating commands (an instruction to one owner) with events (a fact broadcast to unknown readers).

claims.text: Kafka provides ordering guarantees within a partition, not across a topic; a key's hash selects the partition, so ordering scope is chosen by the key.
A consumer's offset is independent of whether the data still exists: retention governs the data, the committed offset only records progress.
Consumer groups distribute partitions among members; a partition is assigned to at most one consumer in a group, which caps a group's parallelism at the partition count.
Compaction retains the latest value per key, which makes a compacted topic a changelog of keyed state rather than a stream of events.

pitfalls: Expecting global ordering across a topic with more than one partition.
Assuming increasing partitions is free — it changes the key-to-partition mapping and thus ordering for existing keys.

claims.text: Avro reads data with two schemas: the writer's schema, used to write the bytes, and the reader's schema, which the reader wants; resolution reconciles them field by field.
For decimal logical types, two schemas match for resolution only if their scale and precision match; scale must be zero or a positive integer no greater than the precision.
For unions, the first schema in the reader's union that matches the selected writer's schema is resolved recursively; if none match, an error is signalled.
When the reader's schema is a union and the writer's is not, the first branch of the reader's union matching the writer's schema is used; if none match, an error is signalled.
Array and map resolution applies the resolution algorithm recursively to item and value schemas respectively.
Avro binary encoding writes no field names or types inline — the payload is positional, which is why the reader must obtain the writer's schema out of band.

snippets.note: Nullable field written as a union with null FIRST and a null default — the ordering the default must agree with.

pitfalls: Writing ["string","null"] with a null default: the default must match the first branch of the union.
Ambiguous unions of several record types, where a reader cannot tell which branch a value came from without inspecting it.
Using double for money instead of a decimal logical type with declared precision and scale.

claims.text: The Confluent wire format prefixes the Avro payload with a magic byte 0x00 followed by a 4-byte big-endian schema ID; the payload itself carries no schema.
Schemas are registered under a subject, and the compatibility policy is enforced per subject at registration time.
TopicNameStrategy is the default subject naming strategy and implicitly requires every message in a topic to conform to one schema.
RecordNameStrategy names the subject by the Avro record fullname (namespace plus name), permitting mixed record types in one topic but checking compatibility per record name across all topics.
TopicRecordNameStrategy combines both as <topic>-<record fullname>, scoping evolution of a record type to one topic.
Schema references (Confluent 5.5 onward) let one schema cite another by reference name plus subject and version.
Broker-side schema-ID validation can reject records whose schema ID is not registered, moving the check off the client's honour system.

pitfalls: Assuming registry outage is harmless: producers and consumers cache schemas, but a cold client cannot serialize or deserialize without the registry.
Leaving the registry writable by every producer, which turns compatibility policy into a suggestion.

claims.text: With acks=all the leader waits for the full set of in-sync replicas to acknowledge the record, guaranteeing it is not lost as long as at least one in-sync replica remains alive.
Enabling idempotence requires acks=all, retries greater than zero, and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection of 5 or less; ordering is preserved for any allowable value.
Idempotence is enabled by default when no conflicting configuration is set; without it, producer retries after a broker failure may write duplicates.
The producer sends when either batch.size is reached or linger.ms elapses, whichever comes first, so linger trades latency for batching efficiency.
A common durability-first starting profile is acks=all, enable.idempotence=true, an increased batch.size, a small non-zero linger.ms, and lz4 compression.

snippets.code:
acks=all
enable.idempotence=true
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5
batch.size=65536
linger.ms=5
compression.type=lz4
delivery.timeout.ms=120000
snippets.note: Durability-first producer profile; batch.size default is 16384 and linger.ms default is small.

pitfalls: Setting retries high without bounding delivery.timeout.ms, so a 'sent' record sits in the accumulator far longer than the caller expects.
Choosing a low-cardinality key and creating a hot partition that no amount of extra partitions will relieve.

claims.text: Durability comes from the interaction of replication factor, min.insync.replicas and acks — none of the three is sufficient alone.
With replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 2, a producer can continue unaffected while a single broker is unavailable provided another replica remains in sync.
Replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas 2 is the common production default, balancing fault tolerance against resource usage.
Under-replicated partitions indicate replicas not in sync with the leader and are a primary cluster health signal.

pitfalls: min.insync.replicas equal to the replication factor: any single broker loss stops writes entirely.
Enabling unclean leader election on a topic whose whole point is durability — it trades committed data for availability.

claims.text: If processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms the broker treats the consumer as failed and evicts it, triggering a rebalance.
Static membership (group.instance.id, KIP-345) preserves partition assignments across a restart within the session timeout, so a rolling deploy need not reshuffle the group.
The incremental cooperative rebalance protocol arrived in Kafka 2.4; CooperativeStickyAssignor lets consumers keep processing partitions that are not being reassigned.

KIP-848's next-generation rebalance protocol is generally available in Kafka 4.0: the broker computes assignments instead of the group leader, and joining consumers receive partitions incrementally. It is enabled broker-side by default, but consumers must opt in with group.protocol=consumer.

A poison pill is a record that can never be processed successfully; an uncaught exception on the consumer thread means the same batch is re-consumed on the next poll, producing an infinite retry loop.

pitfalls: Auto-commit with asynchronous processing: offsets advance past records that were never successfully handled.
Treating deserialization failure as a transient error and retrying forever instead of routing to a dead-letter topic.

claims.text: Kafka's exactly-once semantics combine an idempotent producer (sequence-number deduplication), a transactional producer (atomic multi-partition writes), and read_committed consumers.

A read_committed consumer receives records in offset order but only up to the last stable offset (LSO) — the lowest offset of any open pending transaction — so it sees only committed or aborted outcomes.
The canonical use is consume-transform-produce: output records and the input offsets are committed in one transaction.
Transactions are supported only within a single Kafka cluster; side effects outside Kafka are not covered and need the outbox pattern or idempotent writes.
Long-running transactions block read_committed consumers at the LSO and raise the chance of a transaction timeout.
With transactional offset commits, enable.auto.commit must be disabled to avoid double-committing.

pitfalls: Believing exactly-once extends to a database write or an outbound HTTP call inside the same transaction.
Sharing one transactional.id across instances, which fences the wrong producer.

claims.text: Deletion under compaction is expressed as a record with a null value — a tombstone — which is retained for delete.retention.ms and then removed along with the key's older values.
The cleaner works only on closed (non-active) segments, so the newest data is never compacted immediately.
min.cleanable.dirty.ratio (0.5 by default) sets how dirty a partition's log must be before cleaning runs.
Compaction does not guarantee a single record per key at any moment — duplicates and tombstones can coexist because cleaning timing is non-deterministic.
cleanup.policy can be compact,delete together, retaining the latest value per key while still time-expiring fully cleaned older segments.

pitfalls: Expecting compaction to satisfy a deletion deadline: it is a storage optimization, not a privacy mechanism.
Assuming a compacted topic replays as one record per key — consumers must still be idempotent.

claims.text: Avro records carry a namespace and name that together form the fullname, which some subject naming strategies use as the subject — so naming is an operational decision, not cosmetic.
Avro's doc field is part of the schema and travels with it to the registry, making semantic documentation a schema-design artifact rather than a wiki page.
Decimal logical types declare precision and scale in the schema, and resolution requires both to match — so money precision is a contract decision fixed at design time.
Avro offers timestamp-millis and timestamp-micros logical types, so time precision is an explicit choice in the contract.

pitfalls: Mirroring a database table into an event, which republishes internal refactors as breaking contract changes.
Choosing timestamp-millis and later needing microseconds — a type change, not an additive one.
Embedding PII with no classification, so downstream sinks inherit an obligation nobody recorded.

claims.text: BACKWARD (the default) means a consumer on the new schema can read data written with the latest registered schema; BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE extends that to all previously registered schemas.
FORWARD means a consumer on the latest registered schema can read data written with the new schema; FORWARD_TRANSITIVE extends that across all registered versions.
FULL is both backward and forward compatible against the latest registered schema; FULL_TRANSITIVE against all of them.
The difference transitive makes is that the new version is checked against every previous version, not only the immediately preceding one.
Under BACKWARD, adding a field requires a default so a new reader can supply a value for old data; the reader's default fills the gap when the writer lacks the field.
Aliases let a reader accept a field written under a previous name, which is how a rename is done without breaking readers.
If a writer's enum symbol is absent from the reader's enum, the reader's declared enum default is used; without one, an error is signalled.

snippets.note: An enum default is what lets a future producer add a symbol without breaking today's readers.
Reader-side alias accepts data written under the old field name.

pitfalls: Deleting a field that has no default: old readers still expect it.
Reusing a deleted field's name for a different meaning — technically compatible, semantically a silent corruption.
Adding an enum symbol without a reader default, which fails only when the first record carrying the new symbol arrives.

claims.text: Under TopicNameStrategy a topic implicitly holds one schema, so a genuinely different record type requires either a new topic or a different subject strategy.
TopicRecordNameStrategy scopes a record type's evolution to a single topic, so the same record can evolve at different rates in different topics.
Compatibility policy is set per subject, so criticality-tiered rules are expressed by subject rather than globally.

pitfalls: Putting a version in the topic name and then also evolving the schema, so two version axes drift apart.
Never deprecating v1, because no consumer-migration deadline was ever set.

claims.text: Compatibility can be checked in CI before registration, turning a runtime failure into a pull-request failure.
Broker-side schema validation rejects records referencing unregistered schema IDs, so governance does not depend on every client being well-behaved.
Registry authorization can restrict who registers or evolves a subject, which is what makes an ownership model enforceable.

pitfalls: Global compatibility settings applied uniformly, so a low-stakes internal topic carries the same friction as a regulated one.
Schemas documented outside the schema, where the doc drifts from the contract.

claims.text: The dual-write problem is updating a database and publishing to Kafka atomically without a distributed transaction; the transactional outbox is the standard solution.
The outbox writes the event to a table in the same local transaction as the business change, then a CDC connector streams those rows to Kafka.
Debezium runs as a Kafka Connect connector, capturing changes from PostgreSQL logical replication, MySQL binlog and other sources.

Debezium's outbox.event.router SMT routes outbox rows to topics by aggregate type and uses the aggregate id as the message key, which keeps one aggregate's events in one partition and therefore in order.

pitfalls: Publishing to Kafka inside the database transaction, which either loses events on rollback or blocks on the broker.
Keying outbox events by event id instead of aggregate id, which destroys per-aggregate ordering.

claims.text: A dead-letter queue in Kafka is simply another topic that failed records are routed to, rather than a distinct broker feature.
Failures need classification: a transient dependency error deserves retry, while a malformed record will never succeed and must be diverted.
Because at-least-once delivery is the practical default, consumers with external side effects need their own idempotency key and a processed-event store.
A group's maximum parallelism is its partition count, so consumer scaling is bounded by a topic-design decision made earlier.

pitfalls: Retrying in-line on the consumer thread past max.poll.interval.ms, which converts a slow dependency into a rebalance storm.
A dead-letter topic nobody monitors, which is data loss with extra steps.

claims.text: Every state store is backed by an automatically created changelog topic, which is how a failed instance restores its state elsewhere.
Operations that change the key — a groupBy or a re-keyed join — insert a repartition topic so records sharing a key land in one partition.
The grace period defines how long a window waits for out-of-order records; a record arriving after window end plus grace is discarded rather than processed.
A KTable-KTable join is a non-windowed inner equi-join on primary key producing an ever-updating KTable.
Kafka Streams' exactly-once v2 implementation arrived in the 2.6.0 release and requires broker 2.5.0 or newer.
RocksDB is the default state store, with log-compacted changelogs replicated to Kafka.

pitfalls: Ignoring repartition topics in capacity planning — they are real topics with real storage and real ordering consequences.
Setting a large grace period and then wondering why results are late; grace trades completeness for latency.
Changing a topology in ways that invalidate state stores without planning a reset.

claims.text: By default a serialization error stops the connector task, which is safe but halts the pipeline until a human intervenes.
errors.tolerance=all skips records that fail in supported stages such as converters and Single Message Transforms rather than failing the task.
Connect's dead-letter queue is a configured Kafka topic that failed records are routed to.
Single Message Transforms operate on one record at a time, which is what makes them cheap and what makes them unable to join or aggregate.

pitfalls: errors.tolerance=all with no DLQ configured, which silently discards records.
Reaching for an SMT chain where a stream-processing job is the honest answer.

claims.text: KIP-932 share groups add queue-like cooperative consumption over Kafka topics — roughly a durable shared subscription — rather than adding a queue primitive.
Share groups shipped as early access in Kafka 4.0 (explicitly not for production), as a preview in 4.1, and reached general availability around the 4.2 timeframe.
Ordering is per-partition only, so a design requiring global ordering or arbitrary query is a poor fit for Kafka.
Consumer parallelism is bounded by partition count, which is why classic work-queue fan-out beyond that count historically required share groups or a different tool.

pitfalls: A single shared 'enterprise events' topic that every domain publishes to, which makes compatibility policy meaningless.
Synchronous request/reply over Kafka where the caller blocks on a reply topic and inherits rebalance latency.

claims.text: An ACL binds a principal to an operation on a resource — topic, consumer group or cluster; the authorizer checks stored rules and denies by default when no Allow rule matches.
The authorization flow is authenticate (SASL or mTLS), extract the principal, then evaluate ACLs for the attempted operation on the resource.
SASL/PLAIN is an authentication mechanism, while SASL_PLAINTEXT and SASL_SSL are security protocols indicating whether the connection is TLS-encrypted — they are routinely confused.
Consumers need permissions on both the topic and the consumer group, which is a common cause of a first-deploy authorization failure.

pitfalls: SASL/PLAIN without TLS, which puts credentials on the wire in clear text.
Granting topic access but forgetting the consumer group resource.

claims.text: Consumer lag is the difference between the latest produced offset and the group's last committed offset for a partition — the single most load-bearing consumer metric.
Under-replicated partitions signal replicas out of sync with the leader and are a critical durability health metric.
Lag monitoring requires Describe permission on both consumer groups and topics.
Frequent rebalances are commonly caused by processing exceeding max.poll.interval.ms rather than by genuine consumer failure.

pitfalls: Alerting on absolute lag rather than lag trend, so a healthy backfill pages someone at 3am.
Measuring lag in records when the business cares about time-behind.

claims.text: Partition count is simultaneously a throughput knob, a parallelism ceiling, a metadata cost and a recovery-time factor — it cannot be tuned for one axis alone.
A practical approach is to start modest (single-digit to low-double-digit partitions), measure per-partition throughput on the actual cluster, and size for one to two years of peak.
Stored bytes scale with message size times rate times retention times replication factor, before compression.
Replication and consumer fan-out both multiply network egress, so a widely consumed topic costs more than its produce rate suggests.

pitfalls: Over-partitioning early: partitions are easy to add and effectively impossible to remove, and adding them changes key routing.
Forecasting storage from produce rate while forgetting the replication factor multiplier.

claims.text: A tombstone marks a key deleted in a compacted topic and is itself removed after delete.retention.ms, but cleaning timing is non-deterministic and only touches closed segments.
Because compaction is best-effort and asynchronous, it cannot be relied on to satisfy a deletion deadline for an individual record.
Topic-level ACLs are the practical isolation boundary for regulated data, since a topic is the unit of authorization.

pitfalls: Promising per-record erasure on an append-only log without topic isolation or crypto-shredding.
Long retention adopted for replay convenience, then inherited as a compliance liability.

claims.text: Keying an aggregate's events by aggregate id keeps them ordered within one partition, which is the ordering guarantee an order lifecycle depends on.
The outbox pattern is what makes OrderPlaced publication atomic with the order row write.
Adding a field with a default is the additive change that lets an order schema grow without a consumer migration.
A new consumer can replay from the beginning of a retained topic without coordinating with existing consumers, because offsets are per group.

pitfalls: Modeling order status as a mutable event rather than a sequence of facts.
Cross-domain joins that assume ordering across two differently-keyed topics.

claims.text: Compacted topics keyed by entity id give a durable current-state view that a new consumer can bootstrap from.
CDC via Debezium publishes source-of-truth changes without the source application publishing events itself.
Kafka Streams materializes enriched views into state stores backed by changelog topics, and re-keying inserts repartition topics.
Sink connectors deliver curated events onward, with error tolerance and a dead-letter topic as the operational safety valve.

pitfalls: Treating Avro compatibility as semantic governance: a field can stay compatible while its meaning changes underneath.
PII flowing into a warehouse because the topic that carried it had no classification.

claims.text: A deserialization failure behaves as a poison pill: the consumer re-reads the same batch each poll and lag grows without any record being processed.

Because compatibility is enforced per subject at registration, a breaking change reaches production as a consumer-side failure rather than a producer-side rejection when the policy is wrong for the direction of change.
Rewinding or replaying is possible because retention is independent of consumption, provided the data is still within the retention window.
CI compatibility checks and broker-side schema validation are the two controls that prevent a repeat.

pitfalls: Rolling back the producer while the poisoned records remain in the topic — the consumer still cannot read them.
Skipping offsets to restore service and never reconciling what was skipped.

volatile: Apache Kafka version numbers and per-version feature status (KIP-848 GA in 4.0; KIP-932 share groups early access in 4.0, preview in 4.1, GA around 4.2)
Producer/broker configuration defaults (linger.ms, batch.size, delete.retention.ms, min.cleanable.dirty.ratio, enable.idempotence default)
Confluent Schema Registry default compatibility level (currently BACKWARD) and subject-naming-strategy class names
Avro specification version and logical-type set (recorded against 1.11.x)
Kafka Streams exactly-once v2 minimum broker version
